drills.q: Why doesn't Naive Bayes' false independence assumption prevent it from classifying well?
drills.a: Classification only needs the ranking P(c_A|d) vs P(c_B|d) to be correct, not the individual probability estimates to be accurate. Errors from the independence assumption tend to bias both classes' estimates similarly and often cancel in the pairwise comparison.

drills.q: A classifier reports 96% accuracy on a task where the positive class is 3% of the corpus. Is that trustworthy?
drills.a: No -- a model predicting the majority class for everything scores 97% accuracy on a 97/3 split while catching zero positives. Report PR-AUC and per-class precision/recall/F1 instead, focused on the minority class's recall.

drills.q: Derive the Laplace smoothing formula for Naive Bayes and explain what a very large α does to the model.
drills.a: P(w|c) = (count(w,c)+α)/(Σcount(w',c)+α*V). A very large α dominates the actual observed counts, pushing every word's estimated probability toward uniform over the vocabulary regardless of true class association -- washing out the learned signal. α is a real hyperparameter to tune, not a fixed constant.

drills.q: Your team wants to auto-approve any classification above 0.95 confidence to cut manual review. What do you check first?
drills.a: Whether the model is calibrated at all -- compute ECE and a reliability diagram, specifically checking accuracy within the 0.95+ confidence bin (not overall accuracy). Neural classifiers are typically overconfident by default (Guo et al. 2017), so a raw 0.95 score may correspond to real accuracy well below 95%. Calibrate (temperature/Platt/isotonic) before deriving the threshold.

drills.q: Explain focal loss's modulating factor and why it's a different mechanism from class weighting.
drills.a: FL(p_t) = -(1-p_t)^γ * log(p_t). As the model's confidence in the true class p_t approaches 1 (easy example), (1-p_t)^γ shrinks toward 0, down-weighting that example's loss regardless of its class's frequency -- reweighting by DIFFICULTY. Class weighting reweights by FREQUENCY (a static per-class multiplier), a distinct mechanism often combined with focal loss rather than substituted for it.

drills.q: Design a multi-label classifier architecture for tagging content with amenities, where an item can have zero to many tags, and explain the evaluation choices.
drills.a: K independent sigmoid outputs with per-label binary cross-entropy, not softmax (softmax forces mutual exclusivity that fights a genuinely multi-label training signal). Tune per-label thresholds against a validation set rather than a global 0.5 cutoff. Report both micro-F1 (dominated by common labels) and macro-F1 (equal weight per label), plus subset accuracy if getting every label exactly right matters.

drills.q: Compare the cost/latency profile of Naive Bayes, linear models, and fine-tuned transformers at 10 million documents/day, and state what would change your recommendation.
drills.a: NB and linear models run comfortably on CPU at sub-ms to low-single-digit-ms per document with minor cost differences between them. A fine-tuned transformer needs GPU serving at that volume, a real and substantial infrastructure cost delta. The recommendation changes specifically when the measured accuracy gap on the actual task translates to business value exceeding that infrastructure cost -- not a general preference for either tier.

drills.q: A fine-tuned transformer's accuracy gain over a linear baseline is large, but only on 5% of traffic (a hard subpopulation). What architecture captures most of the value at a fraction of the cost?
drills.a: A cascade: run the cheap linear model on all traffic, route only low-confidence or specifically-hard-category predictions to the transformer for a second pass. This captures most of the accuracy gain where it matters without paying full transformer inference cost on every document.

drills.q: Why is ROC-AUC misleading under severe class imbalance, and what should replace it?
drills.a: ROC-AUC's x-axis (false positive rate) is computed against the large negative class, so even a substantial number of false positives barely moves it, keeping ROC-AUC deceptively high while precision on the minority class collapses. PR-AUC replaces it, since precision is computed against predicted positives directly and shrinks meaningfully as false positives accumulate.

drills.q: Design a text classification strategy for routing user reviews to moderation queues (spam, policy violation, needs-response, routine) at high volume with a tight latency SLA, including how to handle a brand-new policy category with no labeled data.
drills.a: Treat it as multi-label (a review can be both spam and a violation) using independent sigmoids. Start with a linear TF-IDF baseline for the SLA; measure the gap to a fine-tuned transformer and use a cascade if the gap concentrates in specific hard categories. Use class-weighted/focal loss and report PR-AUC per label given imbalance. Calibrate before any confidence-gated auto-routing. For a brand-new category with no data, route just that category through a zero-shot LLM call temporarily while collecting labeled examples via active learning, then fold it into the trained model once enough data exists.
